extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of English literature; poets, critics, and biographers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical observations relevant to composing and judging verse and literary prose (especially Latin/English poetry, heroic couplets, and classical allusion), drawn from a biographical/critical essay on Addison. Emphasizes style, scholarly breadth, originality, and appropriate use of sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of the Latin poets; discriminating perception of style and melody
rubrics_metrics.description: His knowledge of the Latin poets ... was singularly exact and profound. He understood them thoroughly, entered into their spirit, and had the finest and most discriminating perception of all their peculiarities of style and melody; nay, he copied their manner with admirable skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High praise is due when a writer both understands the poets' spirit and can imitate their manner skilfully. Excellence here is measured by accurate sense of style and melodic quality; Addison surpassed most British imitators (Buchanan and Milton excepted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of classical learning (importance of Greek knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: His knowledge of Greek ... was evidently less than that which many lads now carry away every year from Eton and Rugby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A narrow competence confined to Latin poetry limits critical and creative range. To treat subjects derived from Greek sources or art, knowledge of Greek authors (e.g., Pindar, Attic dramatists, Euripides) is necessary for apt allusion, illustration, and full understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of authorities and sources (historians/orators over poets for historical matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spots made memorable by events ... bring to his mind only scraps of some ancient versifier. In the gorge of the Apennines he naturally remembers the hardships which Hannibal’s army endured, and proceeds to cite, not the authentic narrative of Polybius, not the picturesque narrative of Livy, but the languid hexameters of Silius Italicus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing historical or political subjects, rely on the authentic historians and orators rather than poets whose aims and judgments differ. Using poetical sources in place of historical authorities leads to error and misleading impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of style and smooth metrical flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Purity of style, and an easy flow of numbers, are common to all Addison’s Latin poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity, purity, and a naturally flowing meter are virtues in verse. These qualities make poems pleasurable and intelligible and are signaled by evenness of line, appropriate pauses, and avoidance of awkward diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical mastery of metre, euphony, and form (but distinguish from genius)
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of arranging words in that measure, so that the lines may flow smoothly, that the accents may fall correctly, that the rhymes may strike the ear strongly, and that there may be a pause at the end of every distich, is an art as mechanical as that of mending a kettle ... From the time when [Pope’s] Pastorals appeared, heroic versification became matter of rule and compass ... Hundreds of dunces ... were able to write reams of couplets which, as far as euphony was concerned, could not be distinguished from those of Pope himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical proficiency in meter and euphony can be taught and widely imitated; it is necessary but not sufficient for greatness. Critics and writers should distinguish mechanical excellence in form from originality and inventive thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast and tinsel; prefer simplicity and good taste
rubrics_metrics.description: He had learned from [the Greeks] to despise bombast and tinsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good stylistic taste favors simplicity and restraint over inflated rhetoric and ornamentation. Avoid grandiloquence that masks weak ideas; style should serve thought, not distract from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical allusion relevantly to subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: All the best ancient works of art at Rome and Florence are Greek. Addison saw them, however, without recalling one single verse of Pindar, of Callimachus, or of the Attic dramatists; but they brought to his recollection innumerable passages of Horace, Juvenal, Statius, and Ovid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking classical literature in response to particular works of art or cultural contexts, choose allusions from the tradition most appropriate to the object (e.g., Greek poetry for Greek art). Misplaced or narrow allusion can reveal limited learning and a mismatch between reference and subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly rigor and evidence-based argument (avoid credulity and forgeries)
rubrics_metrics.description: He assigns, as grounds for his religious belief, stories as absurd as that of the Cock-Lane ghost, and forgeries as rank as Ireland’s Vortigern ... The truth is that he was writing about what he did not understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure factual claims—especially in essays on history or religion—are supported by reliable evidence. Reliance on spurious or popular but false stories undermines intellectual credibility and leads to error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience accessibility vs learned obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: His lines on the Barometer and the Bowling Green were applauded by hundreds, to whom the Dissertation on the Epistles of Phalaris was as unintelligible as the hieroglyphics on an obelisk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that are accessible and immediately pleasurable to a broad audience may win more popular admiration than highly learned but obscure compositions. Consider intended audience when choosing tone, diction, and allusiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of influences; separate salutary from pernicious effects
rubrics_metrics.description: We think, to discover, in the Spectator, and the Guardian: traces of the influence, in part salutary and in part pernicious, which the mind of Boileau had on the mind of Addison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Influences from predecessors and critics shape taste and technique; consciously adopt what improves your work and reject what diminishes it. Critical awareness helps preserve originality and sound judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and unconscious borrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot help suspecting that he borrowed, perhaps unconsciously, one of the happiest touches in his 'Voyage to Lilliput' from Addison’s verses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for originality but recognize that unconscious borrowing can occur. Compare precedents and be mindful of echoes; when similar material appears, check sources and either acknowledge influence or revise to secure distinctiveness.
